canberra.title: Struggling CIT to offer voluntary redundancies in new drive to cut costs
canberra.snippet: The cash-strapped Canberra Institute of Technology (CIT) is calling for expressions of interest in voluntary redundancies from its workfo...
canberra.content:
CIT students at the new Woden CIT campus. CIT said it was working to ensure students could continue their studies without disruption. Photo: Woden CIT.

The cash-strapped Canberra Institute of Technology (CIT) is calling for expressions of interest in voluntary redundancies from its workforce as part of new plans to put the struggling organisation on a firmer and more sustainable footing.

It is one of several cost-saving measures in its new Sustainable Workforce Program, including deferring new hires and not renewing contracts, and it covers all permanent staff across the organisation. As yet, there are no targets.

CIT was also considering a future overhaul of its organisational structure but did not say whether it was considering cutting courses or merging branches.

The teachers union said the development was deeply concerning.

CIT said that like many public sector organisations, it was managing ongoing financial and operational pressures.

A spokesperson said the program would also include a closer review of all proposed vacancies, a review of fixed-term contracts and contractor engagements and workshops, with the Executive Management Committee to develop a proposed future organisational structure.

“This program is entirely voluntary and no staff will be required to apply or be made compulsorily redundant,” the spokesperson said.

“All permanent staff at CIT are eligible to apply, unless they have already resigned or provided notice of retirement.”

Expressions of interest would be considered against CIT’s operational and educational requirements.

Consultation with staff and unions had commenced, in accordance with the relevant Enterprise Agreement provisions.

“The Board and Executive are committed to supporting students throughout this process and CIT is working to ensure students can continue their studies without disruption, including through the delivery of classes, assessments and student support services,” CIT said.

“The CIT Board has a responsibility to students, staff, industry partners and ACT taxpayers to ensure the organisation remains sustainable and well positioned to meet future education and workforce needs.

“The Sustainable Workforce Program is intended to support that long-term objective while maintaining CIT’s focus on the delivery of quality education and training, delivering on the CIT 10-year strategic plan.”

Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson says the government continues to invest in CIT. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

CIT did not respond to a question about whether it has sought extra funding from the ACT Government.

The 2025 Annual Report showed the operating deficit for the year ending December 2025 had blown out to $28 million, $7 million worse than the 2024 result.

It said CIT had 533 permanent full-time positions and 130 permanent part-time staff.

Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson said CIT had advised its intention to cut costs, including seeking voluntary redundancies.

Mr Pettersson said CIT operations, including employment matters, were managed by the CIT executive and governed by the independent Board.

Mr Pettersson did not respond when asked if CIT had sought a financial top-up, only saying he engaged regularly with CIT on matters relating to their financial sustainability.

“The government continues to invest in CIT to ensure it can deliver public vocational education and training to Canberrans,” he said.

“This includes additional investment in the 2026-27 Budget, including to upgrade ICT infrastructure through the Cloud Campus project, supporting the new Woden Campus, and progressing the EV Centre of Excellence.”

The belt-tightening has come while the embattled CEO Dr Margot McNeill remains on leave with no return date specified.

In the meantime, the Board under chair Tom Rogers was stepping into the breach.

The CIT spokesperson said the Board was taking a more active role in several organisational matters, including those that would ordinarily require CEO approval, to ensure the Institute continued to operate effectively.

The recruitment process for a Deputy CEO had been finalised, and an announcement would be made in the coming days.

CEO Dr Margot McNeill is still on leave. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Australian Education Union ACT Branch president Angela Burroughs said the cost-cutting move would be deeply concerning for many staff.

Ms Burroughs said members had been raising concerns for some time that CIT’s staffing profile has become increasingly unbalanced, with too many resources directed away from frontline teaching.

“If this process genuinely rebalances the workforce so that more resources are focused on delivering high-quality vocational education and training, that will go some way to addressing concerns our members have consistently raised,” she said.

Ms Burroughs said members had been clear that this program must not compromise the quality of education or the diversity of offerings at CIT.

CPSU Regional Secretary, Maddy Northam said the public sector union was deeply disturbed by the announcement.

“The ACT Government should be investing in our public vocational education system, not slashing jobs,” she said.

“Canberrans should feel confident that we have a well-resourced CIT. But with a brand-new campus in Woden, the government needs to tell us if there will be enough staff and students to fill it?”

Ms Northam said the Barr Government had created new measures to make it easier for government agencies to make workers redundant.

“And they are using these measures with abundance: first the City and Environment Directorate and now CIT. Enough is enough,” she said.

“Chief Minister Andrew Barr must intervene and stop the cuts.

“What happens to all the work left behind when redundancies occur? Those remaining will have to pick up the load.

“It’s not fair on members, it’s not fair on workers and it isn’t fair on students.”

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said any redundancies should not target CIT’s teaching workforce, which declined by 68 positions in the last decade while 58 additional staff were added at the senior and executive management level.

Mr Emerson said costs had risen by 38 per cent in that time while program enrolments had dropped by 40 per cent.

“In the last year alone, CIT has cut popular fitness classes for seniors, almost doubled the cost of its highly regarded remedial massage program, and discontinued a critical language education offering for college students,” he said.

“While cutting programs and increasing fees, CIT sent 39 staff to an interstate conference at a likely cost of around $100,000.”

Mr Emerson said it was unclear how some of the decisions CIT has made over the last decade aligned with its core mission of providing high-quality training and education opportunities for Canberrans.

“CIT needs to refocus its expenditure on successful program delivery, rebuilding the Institute’s reputation and improving completion rates,” he said.

canberra.title: Academic fails in bid to overturn finding that failed assessments were discrimination
canberra.snippet: The ACT Supreme Court has refused to take action on a tribunal’s finding that a woman wasn’t discriminated against when she b...
canberra.content:
The Supreme Court has rejected an appeal as “without merit”. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The ACT Supreme Court has refused to take action on a tribunal’s finding that a woman wasn’t discriminated against when she began to fail university assessments.

As of 2021, Dr Loan Dao was completing a masters degree at the University of Canberra.

After passing units in 2021 and 2022, she failed two subjects during the 2023/2024 summer semester and early 2024.

Following those grades, she filed a complaint with the Human Rights Commission against two teaching staff members, accusing them of discrimination, which was then referred to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal (ACAT).

In October 2025, the tribunal found that she wasn’t being discriminated against.

Supreme Court Justice Andrew Muller SC has now knocked back her bid for permission to appeal ACAT’s decision.

In a recently published decision, he described the request as being “without merit” and an attempt to broaden the scope of her complaint from discrimination to a procedural fairness claim.

“It is clear from a review of the decision of Senior Member Hawkins he was not called upon to determine a claim founded in procedural fairness,” Justice Muller said.

“The specific complaint he sought to address was based [on a section of] the Human Rights Commission Act 2005 (ACT).”

According to the original ACAT decision, Dr Dao told the tribunal that by the end of semester two in 2022, she’d started to fail part or all of her assessments.

She lodged a formal complaint with the university in June 2024, but this was dismissed. After this, she filed the discrimination claim with the Human Rights Commission.

When she went to ACAT, Senior Member Walter Hawkins found that she hadn’t established why she was being treated in a particular way, and that her evidence to the tribunal instead focused on how she was being treated.

“In the absence of such evidence, Dao is unable to establish that she has been treated unfavourably because of her protected attributes,” he said.

Canberra’s civil tribunal’s ruling that a woman wasn’t discriminated against by two university teaching staff will stand. Photo: Albert McKnight.

Senior member Hawkins ultimately rejected Dr Dao’s claim that she was being treated unfairly because she was a “woman, Asian and old”.

He also dismissed her argument that the two staff members were jealous that she had a PhD from the Australian National University (while they didn’t).

In the aftermath of that ruling, Dr Dao internally appealed the decision to ACAT, which was dismissed, before she went to the Supreme Court.

The tribunal also heard that as part of marking, the students were given numbers (meaning their work wasn’t identifiable by their name).

He said that she went “to considerable lengths” to get another academic to review her work, but it couldn’t be arranged.

“I also accept that there were other students in the course with a PhD and also older students from a variety of backgrounds including international students, and that many if not most of the students were female,” he said at the time.

In his decision, Justice Muller said that while Dr Dao claimed the tribunal didn’t give enough weight to “objective evidence of the unreliability” of the staff members when evaluating her initial claim, this wasn’t proven in what she put before the court.

“The error of law she relies upon is denial of natural justice and procedural fairness in the refusal “to conduct an external, independent assessment of two of the appellant’s works that were marked as failing by [University of Canberra’s] two teaching staff members”,” he said.

He said that Dr Dao had failed to provide a “reference to any objective measure” showing that her marks were the result of discrimination, rather than of the teaching staff making their judgements about the quality of her assessments.

He pointed to evidence given by the two academics to ACAT, who said they had explained the marking rubrics and also met with her to discuss her assessments.

As part of Justice Muller’s rejection of her request for leave to appeal, Dr Dao will have to pay the university’s costs.

canberra.title: Fuel excise discount is gone and Canberra prices now the highest of all capital cities
canberra.snippet: Canberrans are paying the most for fuel of any capital city now that the Federal Government has removed the fuel excise discount. But it’...
canberra.content:
Prices are on the up: Before and after the excise discount was removed at Manuka (1 August and 3 August). Photos: David Murtagh.

Canberrans are paying the most for fuel of any capital city now that the Federal Government has removed the fuel excise discount.

But it’s a fluid situation, with petrol and diesel prices adjusting around the country to the new ‘back to normal’ structure.

It is expected to take a few days for the full impact of the changes to be felt at the bowser, with prices climbing further at service stations across the nation as the week progresses.

As of Monday morning (3 August), the average price of unleaded petrol in Canberra was $2.10 a litre, with diesel averaging $2.49 a litre.

That compares with Sydney, where motorists pay an average of $1.97 per litre for unleaded and $2.41 per litre for diesel.

The cheapest was in Perth, at $1.95 per litre for unleaded petrol and $2.38 per litre for diesel.

The fuel excise discount was introduced in April as a cost-of-living measure to help offset oil price surges due to the war in the Middle East.

It initially saved motorists 32 cents a litre, but was reduced to a 16 per cent discount in July.

The government has always said the discount would not last.

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said on Monday that the initiative was a big help to households, but was always meant to be temporary.

“The three-month reduction in the excise by 32 cents was a really important measure that benefitted a whole range of people who were vulnerable to increases in the price of petrol and diesel,” he said.

“That included tradies in the outer suburbs, people who weren’t close to public transport, people in the regions, and it had a really positive impact in softening the impact for them.

“When we came to the end of the three months, we, as you know, had a one-month extension at a half rate, and that was an important way of tapering off that benefit.

“The benefit was always intended to be temporary, and so we’ve flagged right from the beginning that it was meant to help people with the worst of the impacts of that crisis, but that it would always at some point come off.”

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has written to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to urge them to be extra vigilant as fuel prices return to normal settings.

“Any price that can’t be explained will face serious scrutiny from the ACCC,” Dr Chalmers said.

“Servos and suppliers are on notice. The regulator will be watching them like a hawk, and they can’t use the return-to-normal settings with the excise as cover for treating motorists as mugs.

“We’ve jacked up the penalties for petrol stations that rip off Australians. They face multimillion-dollar fines if they break the law.”

The Treasurer said it was not Labor’s intention to bring the discount back, but the situation will be monitored and changed if necessary.

“Prices have come up a bit, but they are substantially lower than when we first introduced this excise relief,” he said.

“The excise relief has played a really important role in taking some of the edge off these cost of living pressures that have been turbocharged by a war in the Middle East.

“It was never intended to be permanent. It’s done a really important job, but we can’t afford to continue it forever.”

The Coalition isn’t too keen on returning the discount either, with acting opposition leader Jane Hume saying the government should have found offsets in the budget to pay for it “because reducing the fuel excise is an expensive exercise”.

“We supported them when they said that they were going to taper that back down.

“But again, we asked for offsets, and we even suggested offsets, but again, the government has resisted.”

canberra.title: Teenager, 16, charged after multiple alleged assaults of partner
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This story refers to allegations of domestic violence. A 16-year-old boy is accused of choking his girlfriend multiple t...
canberra.content:
3 August 2026

The teenager allegedly assaulted his girlfriend several times in June and July 2026. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This story refers to allegations of domestic violence.

A 16-year-old boy is accused of choking his girlfriend multiple times.

On Sunday (2 August), an ACT Policing spokesperson said that the alleged assaults occurred multiple times during their relationship.

“Police will allege the boy strangled his 15-year-old girlfriend on four occasions between June and July,” the spokesperson said.

Region is unable to name the boy because of his age.

The boy was arrested at his home around midnight on Saturday after the alleged victim went to police.

He has been charged with four counts of chokes/suffocates/strangles another person and four counts of aggravated common assault.

When he faced the ACT Children’s Court on Monday (3 August), the boy’s lawyer, Amelie McCarthy of Legal Aid, said the two teenagers do not go to the same school.

She also asked that he be excused on the next court date, so he could stay in school.

The prosecutor did not oppose the 16-year-old’s release on bail, but told the court the alleged victim was “concerned about their safety”.

“There is a concern about other family members of the defendant contacting the complainant,” he said.

In response, Magistrate Amy Begley said that the court “can’t put any bail conditions on family members”.

She spoke to him directly as she granted his bail, urging him to follow his bail conditions.

“You need to understand that you are facing some very serious allegations … There is a chance that you’ll be remanded in custody [if you breach those], particularly with regard to any contact with the complainant.”

After the hearing, he was seen hugging a family member before leaving the courtroom.

Under the conditions of his bail, the teenager cannot contact the alleged victim.

He also can’t go within 50 metres of the alleged victim, or a specific address.

The boy will return to court on 31 August. No pleas were entered.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 02 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 02 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

canberra.title: High-rises coming for Hume Circle Precinct after minister ticks off rezoning
canberra.snippet: Planning changes that would allow buildings up to 15 storeys tall in areas around Hume Circle have been approved by Regional Development,...
canberra.content:
Big changes are coming to the area around the Hume Circle roundabout in the inner south. Photo: ACT Government.

Planning changes that would allow buildings up to 15 storeys tall in areas around Hume Circle have been approved by Regional Development, Local Government and Territories Minister Kristy McBain.

The National Capital Authority proposed Draft Amendment 102 to the National Capital Plan in January, saying it would fulfil the original intent of the Griffin Plan for a radial street design and enable the renewal of the Hume Circle Precinct, converting an area of light industry to a mix of residential and commercial uses.

But the proposal immediately came under fire from local community groups and a Griffin expert.

The size and scale of the development, and the changes it would set in train, were heavily criticised by the inner south community and even ACT Government agencies, which said it would create the most densely populated precinct in the ACT and place significant demand on infrastructure and services.

A world authority on the Griffins, Emeritus Professor James Weirick of UNSW, lashed the NCA for rewriting history and failing to provide a detailed case for proposed planning changes to allow high-rise buildings around Hume Circle.

The NCA denied that the proposal arose after it was approached by the Jega development consortium, which has landholdings on the northern side of Hume Circle, but said it has been in talks with the consortium since 2023.

In May, the NCA revised its proposal after community consultation, reducing building heights and density and allaying concerns from nearby residents, such as those in Staffordshire Terrace, by introducing a new land-use category.

But ACT Senator David Pocock said Amendment 102 was still inadequate and he would push for a parliamentary committee inquiry.

The land use structure for the Home Circle Precinct. Images: NCA.

The final version divides the Hume Circle precinct into four sub-precincts – A, a School Sub-Precinct covering St Clare’s and St Edmund’s colleges; B, where the Ramada Diplomat Hotel sits; C, the largest area, from Mildura Street to Dalby Street; and D, between Canberra Avenue and Sturt Avenue, where Staffordshire Terrace is.

It includes completing the outer circle of McMillan Crescent via a new shared, mostly pedestrian route.

There is also a south-north linear park and walking and cycleway to the Causeway from the intersection of Sturt Avenue and McMillan Crescent (Causeway Radial); and a similar east-west link from Hume Place towards Dalby Street through Sub-Precinct C (East West Radial).

In response to criticism that DA102 was too general, there are now more explicit requirements for developers to meet, covering the housing mix, apartment sizes and design, solar access and ventilation, landscaping, streetscapes, access and parking, and active travel.

It says high standards of urban design, landscape and sustainability should define all new development.

Building heights will vary across the Hume Circle Precinct, up to 15 storeys.

On the controversial question of building heights, Sub-Precinct D is a carve-out where a maximum of only three storeys is allowed to “reflect the existing residential character and provide a transition to the lower scale of the surrounding neighbourhood”.

Building heights to the inner circle, surrounding the Canberra Avenue, Wentworth Avenue, and Sturt Avenue intersection, transition to a maximum of eight storeys (no more than 28 metres) in Sub-Precinct C to define the gateway.

On land surrounding the completed Hume Circle (McMillan Crescent extension) in Sub-Precinct C, buildings can rise a maximum of 12 storeys (no more than 40 metres).

Buildings will be reduced in height from a maximum of eight storeys (no more than 28 metres) to Dalby Street as development moves away from the completed McMillan Crescent extension towards lower-scale neighbouring areas.

In Sub-Precinct B, buildings up to eight storeys are allowed, “to respond to the current neighbourhood context”.

But scope for 15-storey buildings (no more than 50 metres or RL617 whichever is lower) remains, except in Sub-Precinct D.

Building proposals that exceed the maximum height “principles” may be considered if they meet one or two of the criteria.

These are if the proposal is for a landmark site, a small footprint tower, which reinforces the urban structure of the Precinct; provides a high percentage contribution of the total development site to open/public space; contributes to housing diversity, including social/affordable housing; offers design excellence and a high sustainability rating; and makes a positive contribution to the community or utility infrastructure and/or public realm.

Amendment 102 provides for the establishment of a Town Square recreational open space for residents and the public, located at the intersection of the Completed Outer Circle and the East West Radial.

The area around it, and an area along the Causeway Radial from Mildura Street, are earmarked for future growth in shops and services.

Amendment 102 will be tabled in Parliament in the coming days.

The NCA will now establish a Steering Committee, with representation from the NCA and the ACT Government, to oversee ongoing processes for the Hume Circle Precinct and to coordinate planning in the broader context of the East Lake Place Plan and the southern region.

Senator Pocock welcomed changes to reflect concerns raised by the community, specifically the reduction in building height to three storeys for construction adjacent to existing residences at Staffordshire Terrace.

But he said much was still lacking, and would advocate for an inquiry by the Joint Standing Committee on the National Capital and External Territories.

He would also urge the NCA to ensure appropriate community representation on the proposed working group.

Senator Pocock remains concerned about the lack of any specific provision for public, social or affordable housing, the importance of maintaining vistas, the absence of any traffic studies and the lack of explicit provision for early education and other critical social infrastructure.

Senator Pocock wrote to Ms McBain in March requesting that the amendment include indicative public transport routes, an overshadowing analysis, road hierarchy, preliminary traffic studies, indicative residential dwelling numbers, typology and composition, indicative streetscape designs and guidance around active frontages, but none of these is included.

australia.title: Kmart sells out of low-cost rival to Meta camera glasses across Australia amid warnings of ‘privacy nightmare’
australia.snippet: Expert says people face being filmed without their consent as $89 Anko smartglasses sell out in stores and online Get our breaking news e...
australia.content:
Kmart has sold out of Anko-branded $89 camera glasses across Australia, which a digital rights expert says presents a “privacy nightmare” as people face being filmed without their consent.

As of Monday, the clear-lens, black-rimmed glasses, which can capture images and record high-definition videos, were sold out at Kmart stores across Australia and online.

The price point at $89 is significantly cheaper than the Meta Ray-Bans that the Anko brand glasses are styled on, which sell from $337.

The Anko glasses run on HeyCyan software, which allows the wearer to play music, answer calls, use an AI assistant, and transfer photos and videos from the device.

The software is used in a range of low-budget camera glasses, from online retailers including Amazon and Temu. Reddit users report that the software is sluggish compared to the software in the Meta Ray-Bans.

Meta has faced significant pushback from privacy advocates since launching the glasses – which some people have dubbed “pervert glasses” – for their ability to record people in public.

Meta’s glasses have a light on to indicate the wearer is recording, but there have been reports of users covertly recording in public, and reports that moderators employed by Meta review intimate footage from the glasses, including of people using the toilet and having sex.

The company last month rolled out an update that disables the camera if the LED light is interfered with, and also reportedly began removing videos from its platform of wearers using the device to harass strangers in public.

New York courts, the US air force and a hacker convention have all reportedly banned people from wearing the glasses.

Meta has said it has sold more than 7m of its glasses worldwide, and has recruited celebrity Kylie Jenner for advertising to push the devices into the mainstream, but the Ray-Bans and the flood of cheap versions of the same technology have concerned privacy advocates.

“Smartglasses with cameras are a privacy nightmare that illustrate how Australian privacy laws haven’t kept up with technology changes,” said Tom Sulston, head of policy at Digital Rights Watch.

“We shouldn’t have elevated expectations of personal privacy when out in public, but we should have some.”

Sulston said it was particularly problematic when in the hands of misogynist social media influencers who use the glasses to make content “of them harassing women – typically in places where we have higher expectations of more sensitive use of video cameras, like the beach”.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner said the privacy regulator was aware of the community concerns and was monitoring the rollout of the new technology.

“Organisations that collect, use or disclose personal information through products or services are subject to obligations under the act and the Australian Privacy Principles where the act applies,” the spokesperson said.

“People concerned about being photographed or recorded by another individual may also wish to seek independent legal advice about whether other commonwealth, state or territory laws may be relevant in the circumstances.”

A spokesperson for Kmart said the Anko glasses “are part of an established and increasingly mainstream category of wearable technology, with similar products available globally from major technology and eyewear brands”.

“As with any device capable of recording images, we expect customers to use the product responsibly, respectfully and in accordance with applicable laws and community expectations around privacy.”

Sulston said that due to the ongoing privacy issues, including how the collected data may be used by the companies producing the glasses, the social backlash would likely continue.

“The best way to lose friends and alienate people will be to be a public specs offender.”

One reviewer on TechRadar said of the Meta glasses this week that although it is his favourite tech of the year so far, he was afraid to wear them in public due to the growing backlash.

“I haven’t been worried about going around wearing my Meta Ray-Ban and Oakley specs in the past, but with growing public anger over the way smart specs are being misused, I have a genuine concern someone will see me wearing them and act violently towards me,” he said.

australia.title: Montessori learning is being shut down at Leah’s school – is a push towards ‘explicit instruction’ to blame?
australia.snippet: Critics say the one size-fits-all approach doesn’t work for all students and there are questions about the body that helped design it Mic...
australia.content:
Michelle’s year-eight daughter, Leah*, has been in and out of hospital since birth with complex medical issues, and Michelle says flexible learning through a Montessori program has allowed her to keep up with school.

She says the Montessori stream at their nearby public school in Victoria has taken a lot of anxiety out of her daughter’s education, due to its “self-directed learning”.

“My daughter has a lot of time in hospital and if you’re coming back to a mainstream school you’re feeling that anxiety because the kids are up to chapter 16 and you don’t know what the topic is and it’s really hard to come back in,” Michelle said.

“With Montessori it’s self-directed learning, so wherever you’re up to you don’t have to compare yourself to the kid next to you … that fits perfectly for her, she just slides back in there like she’s always been there the entire time.”

But the Montessori stream which runs from years seven to nine at the Templestowe College public school north-east of Melbourne is being phased out. Michelle, who helped found the Coalition for Choice in Public Schools group, believes it is because of the state government’s policy forcing all public schools to teach via explicit instruction, a different learning model to Montessori’s.

What is explicit instruction?

Explicit instruction, which has gained traction in recent years, has become a flashpoint in a long-running culture war over educational theory.

The method is teacher-led rather than student-led learning, where the educator will explain a lesson in small chunks, demonstrate the skill, and then ask the student to model it. It’s different to “inquiry-led learning”, where students discover information for themselves.

Education experts say explicit instruction an important method, but not the whole solution to improving learning in schools.

In 2024, Victoria announced the Victorian Teaching and Learning Model 2.0 which mandated explicit instruction, in collaboration with the Australian Education Research Organisation (Aero), a contentious body which has heavily focused on that model.

Under the VTLM 2.0, all Victorian government schools must fully embed the policy in their teaching by 2028 and in some instances will “include retiring approaches and practices that do not align with the VTLM 2.0”.

Since the policy was announced, two Montessori streams in Victorian public schools and one Steiner stream have been shut down or phased out. There remains one Montessori stream in Victoria and five Steiner.

The state education department said it is up to Victorian public schools whether they offer an alternative program such as a Montessori, Steiner or International Baccalaureate stream. In a letter to a parent, seen by Guardian Australia, the department says it, “has not issued any directive in relation to the “retirement” of alternative curricula”.

Mark Powell, director of education services at Montessori Australia, said Aero and the VTLM 2.0 model promulgate a one-size-fits-all approach to teaching, which doesn’t work for all students.

“In June 2024 the government launched VTLM 2.0, a mandatory teaching framework with a hard 2028 deadline, [with] very explicit language allowing for the retirement of non-aligned programs … and then the closure of three programs in the last two years, it looks like a policy design,” he said.

“Montessori is an evidence-based methodology. It’s been internationally recognised over the last century and it’s been proven by many peer reviewed studies to be highly effective for diverse learners including those with neurodivergence.”

At the same time, the federal government has buried a damning independent report into Aero, which the body claims would cause it “serious reputational harm”.

The education department blocked Guardian Australia’s freedom of information request for the report by KPMG, commissioned by Labor, because it could risk damaging relations between the states and commonwealth.

Aero objected to the release, according to the FoI rejection, saying it would “undermine trust in the quality of evidence Aero generates, with a risk that educators and other stakeholders would cease using its resources”.

It said the release could cause “serious reputational harm to Aero … damaging its ability to engage with partner jurisdictions”, as well as harm Aero’s relationships with members, “undermining its ability to fulfil its functions”.

De-professionalising teaching

Alex Bacalja, a senior lecturer who works in initial teacher education at Melbourne University, said teachers, schools and academics had criticised Aero because of its heavy focus on explicit teaching, and accused it of moving decision making and experience from educators to bureaucrats.

“Because Aero claims to know the best methods of teaching, and communicate that knowledge through departments of education, teachers are no longer allowed to decide what is best for the students in front of them at any one time, a bureaucrat has decided that for them … it aims to de-professionalise teaching,” he said.

“It’s like a bureaucratic department telling brain surgeons how to do brain surgery.”

Bacalja was involved in consultation sessions organised by KPMG during the audit.

“I thought there would be a balance of those people who mostly supported Aero’s work and others far more critical. It was all critical,” Bacalja said. “I know colleagues who attended other consultation sessions with KPMG who shared similar stories.”

The Greens education spokesperson, Penny Allman-Payne, said it was “appalling” the report was hidden from the public.

“Aero is meant to be Australia’s national education evidence body and yet they won’t provide to teachers, other educators and school leaders, the evidence of the report into how well they’re functioning … I think that’s pretty appalling.”

The former public school teacher said she had heard criticism from educators and researchers that Aero “takes a very narrow focus on which evidence they use and look at”, and heard other concerns that some of the resources on the website were “insulting” because they were so basic and would have been covered in university.

The federal government is working towards absorbing Aero, the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority (Acara), the Australian Institute for Teaching and School Leadership (AITSL), and Education Services Australia (ESA) into a new “teaching and learning commission”.

The department, in its FOI response, said some education ministers claimed the release of the audit could “prejudice ongoing discussions” about the new commission, but Allman-Payne said the KPMG report should be released because of the new body.

“Information in that report is going to be critical to any decisions that are made … a good process would involve everybody understanding what’s gone well with the bodies that they want to amalgamate and what hasn’t.”

* A pseudonym has been used to protect identity

australia.title: Most Sydney road tolls to keep rising after Transurban accused of blocking reforms
australia.snippet: Handful of tollroads to get one-off price cuts but WestConnex toll to keep rising at least 4% a year Get our breaking news email , free a...
australia.content:
The cost of using Sydney’s biggest toll road will continue to rise at least 4% a year after the multinational private operator was accused of blocking the state government’s push for sweeping reforms.

Only a handful of Sydney’s motorways will receive one-off toll cuts under a deal announced by the state Labor government on Monday, as the tolling bill footed by taxpayers surpasses $1bn.

Eleven of Sydney’s toll roads are run by Transurban, a $47bn company with operations in Victoria, Queensland and the US, with most under contracts granting exclusive operating rights into the 2040s or later.

The deal will see the state pay $850m to widen the M2-M7 tollway, boosting traffic flows, which Transurban expects will increase its toll revenue. The government will separately spend $143m to settle the deal, negotiated over two years.

Under Monday’s deal, Transurban will cut some fares by 10% on the Lane Cove Tunnel and the M2 in July 2027 and the M7 in 2028. The cross-city tunnel toll will be cut by a one-off 20% in 2028 while the eastern distributor’s northbound fare will be cut and a southbound fare added.

Those highways accounted for less than half of the 1m trips recorded each day on average across Transurban’s Sydney network, suggesting most tollway trips would not see a toll reduction.

The Westconnex highway, which alone accounted for 359,000 trips a day by the end of 2025, and the NorthConnex will not get a reduction.

The premier, Chris Minns, told reporters on Monday the government had failed to negotiate a deal for the excluded highways at an appropriate cost with Transurban.

“We weren’t able to get the rate of the dollars that we wanted in exchange for, I guess, what we had to give up,” Minns said.

“We need toll relief now and it’s better to have it at a lower base given the multiple increases that they have through the year.”

Transurban’s chief executive, Michelle Jablko, told investors on Monday the state would have had to spend significant amounts to fund a WestConnex toll reduction.

“Even a small change in WestConnex could cost taxpayers quite a lot,” Jablko said.

Transurban data indicates the average Sydney customer spends nearly $650 a year on tolls. It costs $12.74 for a car to travel the full length of WestConnex and the motorway’s tolls increase by at least 4% each year.

Allan Fels, a former chief of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, led the state’s 2024 tolling review and called for the different roads’ tolls to be standardised so toll burdens would be balanced between Sydney’s west and its wealthier north and east. Jabklo on Monday said sweeping reforms could worsen congestion.

Fels, who was not directly involved in the government’s negotiations, said Monday’s toll reductions represented a “good start”.

But he said Transurban had blocked reform and put profits over public interest. The company declined to comment.

“It’s essentially a financial vehicle, that receives an enormous amount of money, and that’s what it’s all about,” Fels told Guardian Australia.

“[Transurban’s demands] were excessive, completely out of the ballpark … Their whole approach to compensation ruled out some public interest reforms, including on WestConnex.”

NSW taxpayers already pay Transurban more than $100m a year to cover Labor’s cap on tolls introduced in January 2024, covering the difference for motorists spending more than $60 each week.

That figure will more than double to $211m in 2026-27 after the state budget temporarily lowered the cap to $50.

Fels said commuter anger at growing toll bills would force the state to revisit the contracts in future.

“The government deemed it was just too tough politically in the face of resistance by Transurban to deliver the whole package … [but] they hinted they might come back to this,” he said.

Jablko did not directly answer when asked on Monday whether the government had promised it would not amend the contracts in future.

“By working constructively with the government, we were able to deal into what was important to them today and protect the value of the contracts,” she said.

“What government wants to do in the future is always going to be a question for them, but it was really important for us to show up in the right way.”

australia.title: Alan Jones argues ‘rivalry’ and ‘treachery’ but after decades wielding the sword of public opinion, he’s the one on trial
australia.snippet: His legal strategy was apparent from the very first. Jones will, it was explicitly stated, seek to undermine the ‘credibility and reliabi...
australia.content:
Alan Jones has enjoyed decades as the centre of attention, as the wielder of power.

The booming voice, the vast radio audience, the bully pulpit of an eponymous TV show, the great and the good on speed-dial, a staffer in the prime ministerial office dubbed the “minister for Alan Jones”: these were not ancillaries peripheral to the Jones empire, they were central to it.

Even walking into court on Monday, at the epicentre of a glacially moving press pack, it was all about Alan.

That evaporated as soon as he stepped inside the claustrophobic confines of court 3.1.

Here he is simply “the defendant”.

Stripped of his dominance, his control and his voice, Jones is forced instead to listen, as 22 separate allegations are detailed against him.

Jones has pleaded not guilty. He is – as he has consistently asserted – entitled to the presumption of innocence.

…

At first, Jones sat not in the dock but behind his lawyers, with whom he quietly conversed and occasionally showed handwritten notes, recorded with a silver pen in a black notebook.

At one point, Jones was asked to move to another seat across the courtroom.

He would have been in the eyeline of the first witness – Complainant J – and the court wanted Jones moved to a place where he could not be seen by the man who would be the first to detail his charges against him.

From his silence, Jones’s legal strategy was apparent from the very first. He will, it was explicitly stated, seek to undermine the “credibility and reliability” of those who accuse him.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” his barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, told the court, the first thundering sentence of her opening submission.

“Rumours and innuendo have been thrown at Alan Jones for years.”

Jones’s defence would expose, the court heard, “what [the complainants] did not tell the police, what they left out of their statements … but that we have discovered: concoction, contamination and reconstruction”.

“Mr Jones since day one has said he was not guilty of all these charges,” Bashir told the court.

“Mr Jones will have the opportunity to test the evidence in the prosecution case including the credibility and the reliability of the complainants.”

This is a trial over 22 alleged indecent assault and sexual touching offences..

In opening submissions, the prosecution argued a common thread emerged, of people too afraid, too indebted, too ashamed, to speak up in their own defence.

The court heard that Jones had allegedly been financially supporting the family of Complainant A. The then-17-year-old was invited to stay at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls property. There, in a bedroom, he alleges Jones forced himself on him, kissing him and grabbing his penis.

The teenager told no one about it but 10 days later wrote, in a letter to his mother, “Someone in power did something they should not have and I was so worried because of all the help they had offered”, according to the prosecution’s opening.

Another teenager, a star schoolboy athlete from a similarly impecunious background, was given a weekly stipend by Jones, a mobile phone “to keep in contact” and later, a car. Jones allegedly grabbed him on the penis as he drove Jones to his country property, the court heard.

After an alleged incident in which Jones kissed him – un-consented, on the mouth “with a chomping motion … smothering” – Jones is alleged to have told Complainant J “you’ve been a really good boy, I’m going to give you some more money”.

Complainant C worked for Jones at a radio station, and was repeatedly groped by Jones, the court heard. The court heard that, as C drove Jones home from work, Jones would grab C on the penis, rubbing his hand up and down.

The prosecution alleged Jones would talk about C’s penis, “calling him ‘Donkey’ and saying things like ‘It’s not really that big is it?’ and ‘when can I see it?’”

The court was told the prosecution would present as evidence text messages sent by Jones to C, commenting on the “size of his penis, dismay at never having seen C’s penis” and declarations of love.

The court heard C did not invite, nor want to receive, the messages, but felt he had to reply, “concerned about his position in the media industry if he overtly rejected” Jones’s propositions.

Complainant F, who was 17 when he alleges Jones squeezed his buttocks at a public event, told his mother of the assault, but did not report it to police because he “felt nobody would believe his word over the defendant’s”.

…

Complainant J was the first witness to take the stand. A record-breaking junior athlete when he fell into Jones’s orbit, he is now a middle-aged man, but retains a sportsman’s build and singular focus.

Asked to relive his allegations against Jones, J repeatedly took time to compose himself, closing his eyes and asking the court for a moment while he sought to replay in his mind the specifics of incidents, some of them more than two decades old.

J told the court Jones grabbed and squeezed his penis as he drove Jones to his country property, the older man asking “does it feel good?”. In another incident at Jones’s Circular Quay apartment, J gave evidence Jones allegedly hugged him and kissed him without his consent. J’s coach was waiting downstairs in a car for him.

Prosecutor Georgina Wright asked why J didn’t tell his coach what had just happened.

“If I told someone … all of a sudden I would lose everything. I come from a small family, we struggled our whole lives, and I was getting everything handed to me, it was a wonderful life.

“I thought if I told someone what was happening, I would lose everything.”

J told the court he was conflicted by his friendship with Jones.

Jones was generous and supportive, he says, Jones had given him a financial security he’d not known in his life. But there was a price to pay, J said.

“I was fearful of him, but I was also accepting these things from him. And I didn’t want to lose those things.

“The friendship, I would say, was tainted by the things that were going on.

“For me it was a fearful relationship.”

The trial continues.

australia.title: Suspected mass bird flu deaths found in second state as Murray Watt warns ‘this is the beginning’
australia.snippet: Environment minister says Australia has ‘long and difficult journey’ and says more mass mortality events likely Get our breaking news ema...
australia.content:
Aerial surveillance has detected mass bird deaths in a second Australian state in another suspected escalation of the spread of deadly H5 bird flu.

The environment minister, Murray Watt, said on Monday Australia had begun “a long and difficult journey” as CSIRO analysis confirmed Australia’s first mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks off South Australia’s coast.

Hours later, Victorian authorities said aerial observations had identified a “cluster” of dead and sick greater crested terns in the Glenelg River estuary near Nelson and across Lawrence Rocks, in the state’s south-west, over the weekend.

If samples taken from the Victorian birds return positive results, it would be Australia’s second confirmed mortality event from the deadly disease that has devastated wildlife populations globally.

“I want to level with people: this is the beginning of what is likely to be a long, difficult journey in terms of the impacts on wildlife,” Watt said on Monday.

Aerial surveillance over Baudin Rocks identified about 50 dead and 30 sicks birds, the South Australian government said on the weekend.

Samples taken from five greater crested terns and a silver gull were sent to the CSIRO’s Centre for Disease Preparedness and confirmed positive on Monday.

“The reality is, you can’t stop native and wild birds flying around, and you can’t stop wild animals moving around, and that will mean more mass mortality events like the one we have now seen,” Watt said.

“What we can do, and what we have been doing, is build up the resilience of the populations of our native birds and mammals.”

In Victoria, the state’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said aerial surveillance had made observations that were “consistent with what was recently reported in South Australia”.

Speaking to media on Monday afternoon, the state’s chief veterinary officer Dr Graeme Cooke said aerial and ground surveillance in the south-west, near Portland and Nelson, in the past few days showed “a clear increase in the number of dead terns along that part of the coast”.

“Last week we talked about individual detections; the first cases of the H5 bird flu in Victoria. We are now seeing a change as the disease spreads out and has further impacts,” he said.

The region is home to an important breeding colony of Australasian gannets as well as seal colonies and the Glenelg estuary and Discovery Bay, an internationally significant wetland site.

South Australia’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said she was also concerned about a confirmed case of H5 bird flu in a petrel found in the Coorong, one of several new locations where the deadly disease has been detected in the state.

The migratory petrel was one of 18 new cases in SA confirmed by CSIRO on Monday, which included the samples from six birds at Baudin Rocks.

The new cases included a silver gull in Glenelg, two greater crested terns at Troubridge Island, a silver gull at Southend, a greater crested tern at Monarto and six greater crested terns on Pages Islands.

The Coorong is a large area that is home to internationally significant wetlands that support populations of waterbirds and migratory species.

“That confirmed location is of concern because it is where waterbirds are also located,” Bourke said

“So it’s going from seabirds, but also potentially now into where we know a lot of waterbirds are nesting and using this space as a safe haven.”

world.title: Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says
world.snippet: European Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more people The president of the Eu...
world.content:
The president of the European Commission has called for action to strengthen Europe’s borders after tens of thousands of people arrived and quickly left the Spanish territory of Ceuta, triggering a furious row between Madrid and other European countries.

In a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday, Ursula von der Leyen said: “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points, including vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.”

She praised the Spanish socialist leader’s swift handling of the crisis, after the vast majority of migrants left Ceuta and Spain officials began installing a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier at the border ‌with Morocco. “Order has been restored and the returns system in place worked,” she wrote in the letter.

Spain ⁠estimates that about 69,500 migrants ​have returned to Morocco over the past four days, exceeding initial estimates of 50,000 having arrived in the enclave on north African territory on Thursday. Authorities in Ceuta reported that 88 people died trying to reach the territory, while at least 11 deaths have been recorded in Morocco.

Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish enclave, have the EU’s only land border with Africa. There are periodic surges in attempted crossings to both cities, although neither permits onward free movement to the EU as they are outside the border-free Schengen zone.

EU interior ministers will hold emergency talks on Tuesday, which von der Leyen said would be a chance to draw lessons from the crossings.

The EU, she said, should double down on five areas: strengthening cooperation with non-EU countries to prevent migration; stronger external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks; and boosting returns of people with no right to stay.

Italian media reported that Giorgia Meloni’s government wanted to accelerate the opening of offshore migration centres, which Europe’s top human rights expert recently said risk becoming “human rights black holes”.

The EU opened the door to offshore detention centres in June in an unprecedented departure from legal norms as part of a law aiming to increase the deportations of people with no legal right to stay.

Amid heavy criticism of the EU’s divided response to the Ceuta border crossings, von der Leyen stressed that Spain could access EU funds as well as support from the Frontex border agency. So far Madrid has not requested the assistance of Frontex.

The crossings – seized on by far-right politicians across Europe – have exposed deep divisions over migration that have left Spain’s socialist leader isolated.

Over the weekend Sánchez criticised other governments for failing to support Spain, after Italy and Denmark led calls for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen zone. Sánchez said such an attitude was “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest”, contrary to European and humanitarian law “and the principles of solidarity that bind us together”.

Italy and Denmark also organised a letter signed by 20 other EU member states that appeared to blame the crisis on Sánchez’s decision to regularise the status of 500,000 migrants without documents. “We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration,” the 22 leaders wrote, arguing for the need to address “all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularisation of [a] very large number of irregular migrants”.

Academic research has found a weak link, at most, between regularisation programmes and arrivals of irregular migrants.

Michele LeVoy, the director of Picum, an umbrella group that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants, said regularisation programmes had been criticised by EU governments for the last two decades. “If an EU country offers regularisation possibilities, other member states believe that it may invite secondary movement [onward movement to other EU member states] – that is what EU member states don’t want and that explains most likely the harsh response.”

Amid widespread suspicion that Morocco helped fuel the crisis, von der Leyen described the country as “an important strategic partner”, especially in combating “illegal migration”.

Officials said that before the Ceuta crossings, the European Commission was looking to upgrade the EU’s diplomatic relationship with Morocco to a “strategic and comprehensive partnership”. The EU already has similar wide-ranging agreements with Egypt and Tunisia, which include pledges to stem migration, but have been heavily criticised by rights groups.

Von der Leyen wrote: “On anything related to Ceuta and Melilla, we could enhance border management early-warning systems and improve our technical and financial support to Morocco.”

Rights groups said people seeking work or fleeing persecution needed routes to move safely. LeVoy said: “On Ceuta, political games are being played over the lives of people on both sides of the border – those who hope for a better life, and those who are made to fear a so-called ‘invasion’. But what happened in and around Ceuta is fundamentally the result of Europe’s inaction on decent work permits and other regular pathways and the dismantling of its asylum systems.”

world.title: Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing
world.snippet: Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity Explainer: why is Ceuta ...
world.content:
A growing chorus of voices have accused Morocco of helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”.

Spanish officials ⁠said on Monday that an estimated 69,500 people who had arrived late last week in Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa, had returned to Morocco in recent days. Around 2,500 people who had made the crossing were believed to still be in Ceuta.

The extraordinary influx had overwhelmed the city of 84,000 people and set off a political crisis across the EU as some member states laid blame on Spain.

In Ceuta, leaders pointed to the broader picture of what had transpired. “It’s an atrocity,” said Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of the territory. “There are 88 bodies in the morgue, and there are more on the other side of the border.”

He said local people watched the events play out with a mix of sadness, worry and anguish. “People see this not as a migration crisis; it was fundamentally an attack, a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” Vivas told El País newspaper. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco.”

He drew a parallel with May 2021 when Rabat loosened border controls, allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days, during a diplomatic standoff over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.

This time around, analysts have suggested that Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s arch-enemy Algeria could have triggered a response from Morocco.

Speaking on Monday, Spain’s defence minister, Margarita Robles, also seemingly signalled Rabat’s involvement. “Neither Spain nor Morocco can look the other way when it comes to this tragedy,” she told reporters. “I ask the Moroccan government to fully investigate what happened.”

The insinuation appeared to be backed by the preliminary assessment of Spanish intelligence services, who cited suspicions that the influx had not been planned by Moroccan authorities but concluded that Morocco had failed to stem the tide of people rushing towards the border and in some cases had even facilitated their passage.

Intelligence sources told El País that the roots of the influx probably lay in a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported. As the hoax gained steam online, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum until it was completely lifted late last week, allowing tens of thousands of people to stream through.

In Ceuta on Monday, hundreds of people continued to sleep rough on the beach or near Ceuta’s mosques. One local official told reporters that those who remained in the city included 862 unaccompanied minors.

Ashraf, 28, said he had defied his mother’s warnings against crossing into Spain after spotting posts on social media that said the border had been opened. While he had made it to Ceuta, what had followed was a days-long ordeal as he scrambled to find food and shelter while fending off the memories of what he had lived through.

“You might see me smile a little but inside I’m shattered,” the Moroccan national said as he recalled swimming past bodies to reach Ceuta. “There were so many people in the sea. Everyone was trying to grab on to you to save themselves, and you were trying to escape and move forward so they wouldn’t drag you down or drown you. The Moroccan police were pushing us toward the water and telling us ‘swim, swim’.”

Others were desperately seeking loved ones who were missing. One mother said she had been roaming the streets of Ceuta for days, frantically searching for any sign of her children aged 13 and 16.

She had left Morocco alone, finding out later that her two children had followed her by plunging into the sea to make their way around the border.

“I need help,” she said as she held up a photo of a smiling young boy flashing a thumbs-up sign. “Some migrants told me they had seen them in Ceuta, but I can’t find them.”

Across the EU, the crisis in Ceuta had seemingly ushered in a moment of reckoning after a handful of EU countries responded to the crisis by calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Italy said it had suspended passport-free Schengen travel arrangements with Spain for one month, despite the fact that Ceuta is not part of Schengen.

Before an emergency video meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday to address the crisis, Spain’s foreign minister said the country would demand solidarity from EU members after several had, in his view, “fallen short” of what was expected.

“There was a synchronised reactionary international effort that very quickly amplified what was happening, spreading lies and fake news about the integrity of the Schengen area and about Spain’s actions,” José Manuel Albares told the broadcaster TVE. “Unfortunately, these falsehoods have even been amplified by some European governments.”

What had transpired in Ceuta was “very unusual”, he said. “Spain currently has the lowest number of irregular entries on the Mediterranean route,” he added, while Italy “was the country with the highest number of irregular entries in Europe.”

He said he had been in contact with Moroccan authorities throughout the crisis. “They showed a willingness from the very beginning to mobilise police forces to help stem the flow of migrants.”

Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said in a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, that the Tuesday meeting would be a chance to draw lessons from what happened in Ceuta, and she commended Madrid for its swift handling of the crisis. “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points,” she said.

At a meeting of member states on Saturday, the Guardian was told that while Italy and Denmark, with some support from Poland and Sweden, had criticised Spain for what had happened, there was a strong suspicion that the crisis was not an accident but had been coordinated.

There was widespread recognition that Spain could not simply pin the blame on Morocco, given the close cooperation needed to return those who had crossed and, in the longer term, for migration control and security, a source said.

EU states also spoke about the threat of Russian disinformation and how it could exploit the crisis to heighten tensions across the bloc, the source added.

The concerns came into public view late last week when Ukraine’s acting foreign minister said more than 1,500 publications regarding Ceuta had been identified in pro-Russian networks.

“We have detected an intensive Russian propaganda campaign across Europe using pictures from Ceuta to sow destabilisation,” Andrii Sybiha wrote on social media. “This is not about the situation itself but about the way Russia tries to exploit any topic that can benefit its agenda.”

world.title: Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streets
world.snippet: People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects Four days ago, Youssef E...
world.content:
Four days ago, Youssef El Abbas saw an opportunity to reclaim the life he had lost seven years earlier. News was circulating that about 400 people had swum from Morocco to the neighbouring Spanish enclave of Ceuta on the north African coast, approximately 12 miles (19km) across the strait of Gibraltar from mainland Spain.

Here was a chance for the 44-year-old Moroccan father of four to return to Spain, from which he had been deported when his residency expired after the loss of his job in Bilbao in 2019.

El Abbas took a taxi and headed to the city of Tétouan, south of the enclave. While en route, he saw Facebook posts and news reports claiming that the Moroccan authorities were allowing people to pass through their side of the border. That meant that unlike those who had crossed the previous night, he could simply travel overland before swimming for just five minutes across the border from Moroccan to Spanish territory to avoid the Spanish border controls.

He reached Tétouan to find the city completely overwhelmed. “Young men were running through the streets, flooding every corner,” he said. By the time a second taxi took El Abbas to Fnideq, the town bordering Ceuta, he realised that the usual blockades and checkpoints preventing people without European documents from even approaching the frontier had been removed.

“The Moroccan police were shouting at us: ‘Go, go, go! Run now, run into Spain,’” he said. “The night before, they were beating people. But that morning they were letting us through. Nothing made sense.”

Despite the crowds, El Abbas noticed the police were only letting Moroccans cross over. “All the sub-Saharan migrants were being pushed back by force.”

He reached the border at 2.45pm on Wednesday. By 3pm, after a short swim, he was standing on Spanish soil. Not everyone was so lucky.

“In just 10 minutes in the water, I saw four people floating dead in Moroccan waters,” he said. “People were pulling their bodies out.” They were among at least 72 people who drowned or were crushed trying to reach the Spanish territory.

El Abbas is just one of the 50,000 or so people to have crossed into Ceuta this week, in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described as “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.

Madrid has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla – the other Spanish enclave on the north African coast – could not be summarily returned under special rules.

But there has also been speculation that the Moroccan authorities may have opened the border to signal their displeasure at Sánchez’s recent visit to Algeria, which supports efforts to free the disputed territory of Western Sahara from Moroccan occupation.

Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich Millán, said Rabat was not happy about the mass crossing, adding that it hoped those in Ceuta would return.

Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.

In May 2021, Rabat loosened border controls – allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days – during a diplomatic standoff triggered after Madrid allowed a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.

El Abbas said he had never stopped dreaming of returning to Spain, where he had worked mainly in the hospitality sector for 14 years. Since being deported to Morocco in 2019, he has lived apart from his wife and four daughters, who remain in the northern Spanish city of Bilbao, while scraping by with occasional work repairing mobile phones alongside his father.

“I never stopped thinking about coming back,” he said. “In Morocco, I was alive, but I wasn’t really living.”

The return has been bittersweet. When he swam ashore in Ceuta, a Spanish Guardia Civil officer extended a hand to pull him from the sea. But that gesture of aid eventually gave way to one of violence. Three days after arriving, the group of people he was with were surrounded by a military patrol and beaten.

“The same hand that helped me out of the water was the one that later hit me,” he said.

El Abbas’s story is hardly unique. Although more than 48,000 people had crossed back into Morocco by Friday night, hundreds are still sleeping in parks, public squares and on pavements, waiting for a chance to move on or simply to find somewhere to rest. It appears to be virtually impossible for migrants to leave Ceuta for mainland Spain.

Said, 17, from Casablanca, was sitting on a kerb a few hundred metres away. He, too, had joined the Ceuta-bound crowds when he heard that the border was open. But the jubilation had given way to reality and all he had was a bottle of water and the carton of yoghurt a local resident had given him.

The teenager said he was taken to a centre for unaccompanied minors after he crossed, but there were no places available, so he ended up back on the streets. According to a soldier who asked to remain anonymous, the current protocol for the authorities – including the military, the police and the Guardia Civil – is to treat unaccompanied minors as regular migrants and return them to Morocco.

Said and the other teenagers with him said no one would sell them food or allow them into shops and restaurants because they did not speak Spanish.

Three days after the mass influx, Ceuta is slowly trying to recover a sense of normality. By early evening on Saturday, cafe terraces were beginning to fill again and some businesses had reopened their doors. Many of the remaining arrivals are being tended to by Ceuta locals, who walk the streets handing out bottles of water, sandwiches, blankets and clothes. Others stop to ask if they need help or to offer to call a relative.

Such shows of solidarity have been threatened by the arrival of far-right politicians and a neo-Nazi group, all keen to use the humanitarian crisis for their own ends.

“They’re going to exploit our feelings to claim the credit and say they defended Ceuta,” said a local woman called Malika. “We don’t want them here. If they want to defend something, they should go somewhere else.”

Malika, who was born in Ceuta to a soldier who served in the Spanish army, rejected the notion that the city should be defined solely by the political confrontation that followed this week’s mass arrival. But she also acknowledged the pressure on a city of just over 80,000 people. “It would have been an impossible situation for any city,” she said.

Fatima Hamed Hossain, a member of Ceuta’s assembly, fears that the strain created by the crisis has deepened divisions within the city. “Everything we’ve lived through has created tensions between neighbours,” she said. “That’s exactly what feeds the far right.”

As a caravan of people returned back over the border, Said’s mind was on the future. His goal is simple: get a place in a protection centre, spend the next year learning Spanish and, once he turns 18, find work as a barber. What he fears most is ending up without legal documentation and seeing that plan collapse before it has even begun.

Leaving is not on his agenda, however. “All I need,” he said, “is a chance.”

world.title: Anti-LGBTQ+ laws are on the rise across west Africa, campaigners warn
world.snippet: Activists in the region say politicians regard LGBTQ+ people as ‘the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power’ A growing number of west...
world.content:
A growing number of west African countries are implementing or strengthening anti-LGBTQ+ laws, amid local political pressures and a global pushback against LGBTQ+ rights.

In March, Senegal doubled the maximum prison sentence for gay sex to 10 years and criminalised the “promotion” of homosexuality. Niger criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February, the first time same-sex intimacy had been outlawed in the country.

Mali and Burkina Faso, which neighbours Niger, also criminalised same-sex relations for the first time in the last two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.

In June, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed a law criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which hasn’t been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of a bill that was first introduced in 2021.

“What I see in all of them is a political opportunism,” said Anthony Oluoch of Pan Africa ILGA, a continental LGBT+ rights campaign group.

In some countries, he said, the new or harsher laws had been backed by religious groups and campaigns for “family values”, while in Burkina Faso, whose population is predominantly Muslim, the law was framed as boosting its sovereignty in opposition to the west. “Underneath that all, there’s a lot of transnational reinforcement,” Oluoch added.

LGBTQ+ people “are the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power”, said an activist in Burkina Faso, who could not be named for her security.

The impact on the community, even before the law was implemented, has been devastating, activists said. Thirteen transgender women were detained without trial from June to November last year, a HIV worker said, with the women reporting they had been beaten by a military unit that imprisoned them. After the law was passed, there have been at least two sets of convictions.

Police are entrapping LGBTQ+ people on social media and demanding they denounce other community members, said the HIV worker, who fled the country in May after he was named by someone who had been arrested.

Despite military president Ibrahim Traoré’s anti-western rhetoric, Burkina Faso has also caught the eye of anti-LGBTQ+ campaigners that include conservative, western Christian groups.

The African Inter-Parliamentary Conference on Family Values and Sovereignty, a forum that many argue has influenced anti-LGBTQ+ laws on the continent, will be held in Burkina Faso and then Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) next year, it was announced this year.

The first three conferences were held annually in Uganda, in east Africa, beginning in 2023. Uganda imposed the death penalty for some same-sex sexual acts that year.

According to US-based international reproductive rights organisation Ipas, the annual gatherings are supported by Family Watch International (FWI), an Arizona-based Christian campaign group that opposes abortion and comprehensive sex education (CSE). Also in attendance has been Dutch-founded lobby group Christian Council International, which promotes similar views.

At this year’s conference, hosted by Ghana’s parliament in June, the draft African Charter on Family Sovereignty and Values treaty was drawn up. It condemns abortion and CSE, states that gender is either male or female, and asserts that parental rights supersede children’s. A draft copy was published on FWI’s website.

The anti-LGBTQ+ bill passed by Ghana’s parliament is a “very effective political tool”, supported by powerful religious organisations in the country, said Amanda Odoi, a researcher at the University of Cape Coast.

Nonetheless, Odoi added: “These international actors were very key in empowering, supporting, funding, financing and giving voice to the anti-LGBT campaign.”

She noted the Ghana bill’s similarity to Uganda’s law, as well as its “alphabet soup” – the bill uses the acronym “LGBTTQAP+” – that includes words like “questioning” not commonly used in Ghana.

Bringing this year’s African parliamentary conference to Ghana was a deliberate decision due to the country’s influence on the continent, said Ebenezer Peegah, executive director of Rightify Ghana, an NGO that supports LGBTQ+ people.

“Ghana has a lot of credentials that Uganda does not have … some clout that other countries in Africa do not have,” said Peegah, listing Ghana’s stable democracy, free and fair elections and relative press freedom.

Across west Africa, LGBTQ+ people are suffering the consequences of the new and harsher laws. In Senegal, the law is also hindering HIV prevention for men who have sex with men and transgender women, who have higher rates of HIV prevalence, as well as lawyers representing LGBTQ+ people, said Marame Kane, a French-Senegalese activist based in Paris.

About 100 Senegalese people fled to the Gambia this year, although most had to return to Senegal as they had no money, according to a Gambian HIV worker.

Same-sex relations are already punishable with up to life in prison in the Gambia, while transgender women are criminalised by a cross-dressing ban. However, the HIV worker worried that the government could strengthen the laws, making HIV services even harder to provide.

The crackdown in Senegal had also increased homophobia in the Gambia, he said, adding, “Gambia and Senegal share the same culture, the same religion, literally everything.”
